mcqs.q: Diabetes mellitus is characterised by hyperglycaemia due to:
opts: Absolute or relative insulin deficiency, resistance, or both
mcqs.explain: DM is a metabolic disorder with hyperglycaemia from absolute or relative insulin deficiency, insulin resistance, or both.

mcqs.q: Which type accounts for about 90% of all diabetes?
mcqs.explain: Type 2 diabetes makes up about 90% of cases; type 1 is 5–10%.

mcqs.q: Type 1 diabetes is fundamentally due to:
opts: Absolute insulin deficiency from β-cell destruction
mcqs.explain: Type 1 is an absolute insulin deficiency from autoimmune β-cell destruction (HLA-DR3/4, viral triggers).

mcqs.q: Type 2 diabetes is predominantly characterised by:
opts: Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency
Complete absence of insulin from birth
An autoimmune attack on islet cells
A viral destruction of the pancreas
mcqs.explain: Type 2 is predominantly insulin resistance with a relative (lesser) insulin deficiency, linked to obesity, age >40 and family history.

mcqs.q: Gestational diabetes is caused by:
opts: Placental hormones interfering with insulin (2nd–3rd trimester)
mcqs.explain: Gestational diabetes appears in the 2nd/3rd trimester when placental hormones interfere with insulin; it raises the future risk of type 2.

mcqs.q: Which drug class can cause SECONDARY diabetes?
mcqs.explain: Secondary diabetes can be caused by corticosteroids, thiazide diuretics and beta-blockers, by endocrine disorders, and by pancreatic disease.

mcqs.q: The classic '3 Ps' of hyperglycaemia are:
mcqs.explain: Polyuria (excess urination), polydipsia (thirst) and polyphagia (hunger) are the classic symptoms, with blurred vision, weight loss and frequent infections.

mcqs.q: Polyuria begins once the blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold of about:
mcqs.explain: When serum glucose rises above the renal threshold for reabsorption (~180 mg/dL), glucose spills into urine, causing osmotic polyuria.

mcqs.q: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is characteristically accompanied by:
opts: The smell of acetone on the breath
mcqs.explain: DKA is a medical emergency with confusion/coma, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain and the smell of acetone on the breath; it is the first presentation in ~25% of new type 1.

mcqs.q: Hypoglycaemia is generally defined as a blood glucose of:
mcqs.explain: Hypoglycaemia is a glucose ≤70 mg/dL, caused by a skipped meal, extra activity, or too much insulin/glucose-lowering medication.

mcqs.q: Which are the MICRO-vascular complications of diabetes?
opts: Stroke, MI and peripheral vascular disease
mcqs.explain: Micro-vascular complications are neuropathy, retinopathy and nephropathy; macro-vascular ones are CAD, peripheral vascular disease and stroke.

mcqs.q: Glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA1c) reflects the average blood glucose over the preceding:
mcqs.explain: HbA1c reflects glucose concentration over the previous 2–3 months; ≥6.5% is diagnostic of diabetes.

mcqs.q: By ADA criteria, which HbA1c value is diagnostic of diabetes?
mcqs.explain: Diabetes: HbA1c ≥6.5% (normal 4–5.6%, pre-diabetes 5.7–6.4%); or fasting ≥126 mg/dL, or 2-h OGTT ≥200 mg/dL.

mcqs.q: The ADA fasting plasma glucose threshold for diagnosing diabetes is:
mcqs.explain: A fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) is diagnostic; a random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms also qualifies.

mcqs.q: The mainstay of treatment for type 1 diabetes is:
mcqs.explain: Type 1 requires lifelong insulin (short/rapid/long-acting, injections or a pump); its main side effect is hypoglycaemia.

mcqs.q: The usual first-line oral drug for type 2 diabetes is:
mcqs.explain: Type 2 is managed with lifestyle modification plus oral hypoglycaemics, typically metformin first, ± insulin later.

mcqs.q: The most important dental/periodontal consequence of poorly controlled diabetes is:
opts: Increased risk and severity of periodontitis, with slow healing
mcqs.explain: Diabetes has no specific oral lesion but predisposes to gingivitis/periodontitis, increases infection risk and slows healing.

mcqs.q: Which oral infection is more common in diabetics and presents as white patches with a burning sensation?
mcqs.explain: Oral candidiasis (thrush) causes painful white patches, bad breath, burning and altered taste; control of blood glucose and antifungals help.

mcqs.q: Mucormycosis, an invasive fungal infection, is most associated with:
mcqs.explain: Mucormycosis is a rare, invasive fungal infection occurring in uncontrolled diabetics, especially during diabetic ketoacidosis.

mcqs.q: Circumoral paraesthesia (numbness around the mouth) in an insulin-treated patient is an early warning of:
mcqs.explain: Circumoral paraesthesia is a critical, often early symptom of impending hypoglycaemia in insulin-treated patients.

mcqs.q: Grinspan syndrome is the triad of:
mcqs.explain: Grinspan syndrome = diabetes + oral lichen planus + hypertension (lesions may also be drug-related).

mcqs.q: The antibiotic of choice for treating infections in a diabetic patient is:
mcqs.explain: Amoxicillin is preferred (infection aggravates hyperglycaemia); tetracyclines and ciprofloxacin enhance the hypoglycaemic effect of medication.

mcqs.q: The analgesic of choice in a diabetic patient is:
mcqs.explain: Paracetamol or codeine is preferred; NSAIDs are used with caution (renal damage, GI bleeding, especially with low-dose aspirin).

mcqs.q: Which drug should be AVOIDED as it disturbs diabetic control by raising blood glucose?
mcqs.explain: Corticosteroids increase blood glucose and disturb diabetic control; they should be avoided where possible.

mcqs.q: Regarding local anaesthetic with adrenaline in a diabetic patient:
opts: It can be used safely for minor procedures with no special precaution
It must always be given without vasoconstrictor
mcqs.explain: LA containing adrenaline can be used safely with no special precaution for non-surgical or short minor procedures (e.g. simple single extractions).

mcqs.q: Why should a diabetic patient be raised slowly from the supine position in the dental chair?
opts: Autonomic neuropathy can cause orthostatic (postural) hypotension
mcqs.explain: Autonomic neuropathy predisposes to orthostatic hypotension, so the supine patient should be raised upright slowly.

mcqs.q: Dental appointments for diabetic patients are best scheduled in the:
mcqs.explain: Morning appointments are advisable; for well-controlled patients minor surgery is done within 2 hours of breakfast and the morning insulin dose.

mcqs.q: During dental surgery in a diabetic, the target blood glucose range is about:
mcqs.explain: Target perioperative glucose is 6–10 mmol/L (108–180 mg/dL), acceptable 4–12; starvation is minimised to avoid hypoglycaemia.

mcqs.q: A poorly controlled diabetic patient needing a non-emergency extraction should be:
opts: Referred to control blood glucose before treatment
Treated immediately with extra insulin in the chair
mcqs.explain: Poorly controlled diabetics should be referred for glycaemic control before non-emergency treatment; elective care is delayed until stable.

mcqs.q: Postoperatively, which oral hypoglycaemic should NOT be restarted if the eGFR is below 30 mL/min?
mcqs.explain: Oral hypoglycaemics are restarted with the first meal, but metformin should not be used if the eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m² (lactic-acidosis risk).

saqs.q: Define diabetes mellitus and contrast type 1 with type 2.
saqs.a: Metabolic disorder with hyperglycaemia from insulin deficiency/resistance. Type 1 (5–10%): absolute deficiency, β-cell destruction (autoimmune), young. Type 2 (90%): insulin resistance + relative deficiency, older/obese.

saqs.q: List the classic symptoms of hyperglycaemia.
saqs.a: Polyuria (above renal threshold 180 mg/dL), polydipsia, polyphagia, blurred vision, weight loss, fatigue, frequent infections (genital Candida) and slow wound healing.

saqs.q: Compare the acute complications of diabetes.
saqs.a: DKA: emergency, type 1, acetone breath, vomiting, coma. Hyperosmolar non-ketotic state: glucose >600 mg/dL, dehydration, type 2. Hypoglycaemia: glucose ≤70 mg/dL (too much insulin/skipped meal).

saqs.q: State the ADA diagnostic criteria for diabetes.
saqs.a: Any one of: HbA1c ≥6.5%; fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL; 2-h OGTT ≥200 mg/dL; or random ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms. HbA1c reflects glucose over 2–3 months.

saqs.q: List the oral manifestations of diabetes.
saqs.a: Periodontitis (key), xerostomia (caries/ulcers), oral candidiasis, sialosis, hypogeusia, mucormycosis (uncontrolled/DKA), and circumoral paraesthesia (early hypoglycaemia). Grinspan = DM + lichen planus + HTN.

saqs.q: Summarise drug choices for a diabetic dental patient.
saqs.a: Antibiotic of choice amoxicillin; analgesic paracetamol/codeine (NSAIDs with caution); avoid corticosteroids (raise glucose); LA with adrenaline is safe for minor procedures.

saqs.q: Outline the dental-surgery precautions in a diabetic patient.
saqs.a: Morning appointments, minimise starvation, monitor glucose (before/hourly/after), aim 6–10 mmol/L. Well-controlled: operate within 2 h of breakfast + insulin; poorly controlled → refer first; raise supine patient slowly (orthostatic hypotension).
